blocks.text: 两党对数据中心建设的反对，是这种反弹最具体的体现。周二选票上的44项地方数据中心禁令中有43项获得通过，向AI公司发出了明确信号：在全国各地建设数据中心无疑将变得更加困难。在数据中心建设增长最快的地区之一、也是关键摇摆州的得克萨斯，当选州长Gina Hinojosa表示，她计划“发布暂停令——禁止——所有数据中心审批，直到立法机构通过保护得州人的法律”。其他几个关键州也做出了类似承诺。

blocks.text: “数据中心是一个切入点，让人们从更广泛的企业问责视角来看问题：‘我的账单在涨，为什么？’”非营利科技行业监督机构The Tech Oversight Project副执行主任Kyle Jacobs-Morse说。“人们发现罪魁祸首是大型科技公司。”他还说，尤其是在得克萨斯、佐治亚和俄亥俄州的州长竞选中，民主党竞选团队把数据中心可能引发的本地问题列为优先议题，包括给当地居民、社区和州政府带来的“溢出成本”。

blocks.text: 但科技行业内外的一些人对这个消息的看法比其他人更积极。一位X用户写道，“我们*也许*又回到了作为一个国家理性、稳健掌舵的状态，能够真正发挥领导作用”，另一些人则写道，最近的结果可能有利于防止AI泡沫破裂。Glen Echo Group首席执行官、Orchestra合伙人Katie Barr说，她不会“过度解读”这一结果，将其视为对科技的压倒性排斥，而更应看作是对“可负担性、就业、安全，以及人们能否对社区和生活中发生的事情有发言权”的一次清算。

blocks.text: AI 安全也很可能会被重新审视。参议员 Mark Warner（弗吉尼亚州民主党）在竞选时主张 AI 安全政策并成功连任；参议员 Jon Ossoff（佐治亚州民主党）在周二的胜选演讲中说：“硅谷的巨头们给自己挖地堡，还警告说他们正在创造的人工智能有让人类灭绝的风险。”一些 AI 安全立法已经在酝酿中，比如参议员 Bernie Sanders（佛蒙特州独立派）和众议员 Greg Casar（得克萨斯州民主党）9 月提出的“禁止超级智能”法案。

blocks.text: On Tuesday night, Democrats made history as they took control of the House and the Senate, and a blue wave swept through traditionally red and swing states — with the nation’s first Black woman governor elected in Georgia, the country’s first Native American woman governor elected in New Mexico, and a Maine Senator ceding to a Democrat after 30 years in office. In these and other campaigns, one theme kept coming up: holding AI companies accountable to the American people. Now, the AI industry is left considering the prospect of regulation, data center construction slowdowns, and more.

blocks.text: Tuesday’s results were a “total repudiation” of the AI field, says Wes McEnany, the former Deputy Labor Policy Director of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, & Pensions, who now works with the nonprofit Future of Life Institute. He said that AI touches “every aspect of people’s lives,” whether they’re applying for jobs, using social media, or even paying electricity bills while living near a data center, and that they’re tired of not having “any agency in that conversation.”

blocks.text: The bipartisan backlash against data center construction is the most tangible manifestation of that backlash. It’s going to be unquestionably more difficult to build them across the country, after 43 out of 44 local data center moratoria on Tuesday’s ballots passed, sending a clear message to AI companies. In Texas, the fastest-growing data center buildout area and a key battleground state, governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she plans to “issue a moratorium — a ban — on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans.” Similar promises have been made in a handful of other key states.

blocks.text: “Data centers are an entry point to looking at this broader corporate accountability lens of, ‘My bill is going up, why?’” said Kyle Jacobs-Morse, deputy executive director at The Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit tech industry watchdog. “People found that it was big tech companies that were the culprit.” He added that particularly in the gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, Democratic campaigns prioritized potential local issues stemming from data centers, including “spillover costs” for local residents, communities, and state governments.

blocks.text: “I do think we’ll hear more questions about who benefits from and who pays for AI, especially as it pertains to infrastructure, but what I’m more curious about is what changes we can expect around regulation,” said François Ajenstat, CEO and founder of Golden Analytics.

blocks.text: Experts say the midterm results have likely ended Trump and congressional Republicans’ repeated attempts to bar state-level AI restrictions. Thomas considers the idea “completely dead,” while McEnany said “any member who votes to wipe out state AI laws is going to be looking for a job in the next [election].” Jacobs-Morse expects to generally see more “tech accountability bills.”

blocks.text: OpenAI recently began calling its data centers “compute campuses,” and President Trump in September attempted to change the name of AI as a technology to “super intelligence.” But midterm results suggest that a significant portion of American voters aren’t buying the rebranding efforts.

blocks.text: But some in and around the tech industry are taking the news more positively than others. One X user wrote that “we’re *maybe* back to being a rational, steady hand as a country and can really lead,” while others wrote that the recent results could be good for preventing an AI bubble burst. Katie Barr, CEO of Glen Echo Group and a partner at Orchestra, said she wouldn’t “over-read” the results as an overwhelming tech rejection but rather a reckoning on “affordability, jobs, safety, and whether people have a say in what’s happening in their communities and their lives.”

blocks.text: There will also likely be a reckoning on AI safety. Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) was reelected after campaigning for AI safety policy, and in a victory speech Tuesday by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Ossoff said, “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.” Some AI safety legislation is already being considered, like the bill to “ban superintelligence” introduced in September by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas).

blocks.text: President Trump has dismissed the idea of a safety crisis in AI as a “hoax,” writing on social media that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” After the midterms, however, Republican lawmakers will need to decide whether to fall in line or negotiate with Democrats on safety-focused policy measures. Either way, Adam Kovacevich, founder and CEO of Chamber of Progress, a pro-tech industry advocacy group, said he expects AI safety legislation to continue to happen in blue states.
